newsitem.title: BRAZIL: POLL - Banks show confidence in Brazil forex plan.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Banks show confidence in Brazil forex plan.

text.p: Most U.S. and Brazilian banks are confident Brazil can resist a sharp currency devaluation over the next two years and stick with its controversial crawling peg forex system, according to a Reuters poll.
The survey of 40 banks, brokerages and research houses found that the highest probability of a 15-20 percent, overnight devaluation was just 24 percent in the first half of 1999.

"The results show that in the most critical semester people think the chance of not having a devaluation is nearly 80 percent. That is a pretty good sign of confidence in the current system," said Carlos Kawall, Citibank's chief Brazil economist.

The poll, conducted from Aug 11-13, found that most banks felt there was virtually no chance of a sharp devaluation prior to the October 1998 presidential election, when President Fernando Henrique Cardoso is widely expected to become the first incumbent Brazilian president to be re-elected.
Cardoso's popularity is based largely on a successful, three-year inflation slashing drive, the Plano Real, that has been anchored by a strong real, Brazil's currency.
The poll found that on average, banks said the chance of an overnight devaluation in the current semester was just 3 percent, rising to 4 percent in the first half of 1998.
Probability rose to 10 percent in the second half of 1998, but the rise was seen reflecting devaluation risk after the October election that semester.
Economists said the results reveal widespread confidence that the government, not the market, will remain in control of forex policy.

"This clearly shows that people think the government will lead a devaluation and not the market because of the higher probability given after the election, which means the government can decide when it wants to act," said Dany Rappaport, chief economist at Banco Santander in Brazil.
Devaluation risk, however, was seen very low and four respondents, or 10 percent of the total, said the probability of a steep devaluation was zero in each of the next six semesters.

"The track record of the Central Bank has shown that it is pretty adept at moving the current crawling peg system and that it can sit there with some degree of confidence and mini-devalue the real," said Chip Brown, chief economist for Latin America at Morgan Stanley-Dean Whitter.
Brown was among the four respondents who saw no chance of a 15-20 percent devaluation through the first half of 2000.

Still, Brazil's burgeoning current account deficit and failure to rein in government spending have put increasing pressure on the Central Bank to speed depreciation of the real, which many say is overvalued by as much as 25 percent against the U.S. dollar.

The bank currently depreciates the real by about 0.55 percent a month through adjustments in a narrow "mini" band within which the real trades against the dollar. The bank aims for an annual 7 percent to 8 percent nominal devaluation.

But critics like Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor Rudiger Dornbusch say the crawling peg, mini-band system will never bring the real down to its true value. Only at that level, they argue, can Brazil solve its current account woes and spur economic growth.
Dornbusch's prescription: a once-off, 15-20 percent devaluation now to avoid economic chaos down the road.

While the poll found that most economists think Dornbusch's remedy is a bit draconian, many shared his worries over the current account gap, which is expected to top 4.5 percent of gross domestic product this year.
Some 20 percent of respondents said they believed devaluation risk was 50 percent or more, meaning they thought it would happen, in the first half of 1999.
This was interpreted as an overwhelming fear by one-fifth of respondents that trade and current account deficits would force a devaluation in the medium-term.
The most noteworthy anomalies were responses by two participants who gave far higher-than-average risks of devaluation in the current semester.

"No one denies that the exchange rate is overvalued. If a devaluation is inevitable then it would make more sense to do it now when market climate is favourable than in the first half of next year, which is an election year," said an economist at a Brazilian investment bank.
He believed there was a 40 percent chance of a devaluation this semester.

An economist at a U.S. bank that gave a 20 percent chance this semester said: "It is better to work on a sick patient now while he is still a little healthy than to wait until his condition is terminal."
